lesson.title: Maximum Profit: Where Marginal Revenue Meets Marginal Cost
lesson.summary: Build a profit function from revenue and cost, then show that the calculus condition for maximum profit is exactly the economic rule that marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
lesson.body:
Profit is revenue minus cost, P(x) = R(x) - C(x), where x is the number of units produced and sold. Because profit is built from two simpler functions you likely already optimized separately, minimizing cost and tracking marginal profit, maximizing profit is really about combining those two ideas: differentiate the combined function, and notice that P'(x) = R'(x) - C'(x) is exactly marginal revenue minus marginal cost.

Suppose a company sells a product at a price that depends on how many units it produces, p(x) = 150 - x dollars per unit, valid for 0 <= x <= 150 units (beyond 150 the price would go negative, which is not meaningful). Revenue is price times quantity: R(x) = x * p(x) = x(150 - x) = 150x - x^2. The cost to produce x units is C(x) = 2000 + 30x, representing 2000 dollars of fixed costs (equipment, rent) plus 30 dollars of variable cost per unit.

Profit is P(x) = R(x) - C(x) = (150x - x^2) - (2000 + 30x) = -x^2 + 120x - 2000. Differentiate: P'(x) = -2x + 120. Setting P'(x) = 0 gives x = 60. It is worth pausing to see this condition in its economic form: R'(x) = 150 - 2x is marginal revenue, and C'(x) = 30 is marginal cost. Setting marginal revenue equal to marginal cost, 150 - 2x = 30, also gives x = 60, exactly the same answer. This is not a coincidence, P'(x) = 0 and R'(x) = C'(x) are algebraically the same statement.

Verify with the second derivative: P''(x) = -2, which is negative for every x, so the profit function is concave down across its entire domain, confirming that x = 60 is not merely a local maximum but the global maximum on the whole domain.

Compute the maximum profit: P(60) = -3600 + 7200 - 2000 = 1600 dollars. As a check against the domain's boundaries, P(0) = -2000 (pure loss from fixed costs with no revenue) and P(150) = -22500 + 18000 - 2000 = -6500 (also a loss, since price has dropped to zero at that production level). Both endpoints are far worse than the interior maximum, confirming x = 60 truly dominates the entire feasible range.

The economic intuition matches the calculus perfectly: as long as each additional unit brings in more revenue than it costs to produce (marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost), producing more increases profit. Once marginal cost overtakes marginal revenue, every additional unit actually shrinks profit. The maximum sits precisely where those two rates cross, which is exactly what setting P'(x) = 0 finds.
